data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'critical attitude' that maximizes verisimilitude (truth-likeness) without assigning probability, accepting the cost that this preference offers no guarantee of practical success or future reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implies an expectation that the future will resemble the past.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' cannot be defined without probabilistic assumptions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'critical attitude' itself relies on an inductive habit of mind.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of corroboration (a report of past performance) and the pragmatic decision to prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests. This preference is rational not because it predicts future success (which would be induction), but because the highly corroborated theory is currently the best candidate for having high verisimilitude. The 'cost' is acknowledging that this preference is a regulative ideal rather than a justification for action in the sense of ensuring safety or utility.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
